speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: JAPANESE PEACE SETTLEMENT-PRESS REPORT FROM LONDON
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. An Associated Press dispatch from London, published this morning in the Ottawa Citizen, states:
Britain and her four dominions have decided to stage a conference to formulate an empire peace policy for Japan, a dominions office spokesman disclosed today.
In addition to this, there have been dispatches, as the minister knows, during the last week or two with regard to a possible peace conference for Japan. It would be very helpful if the minister could give the house a statement with regard to the question.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): The first paragraph of the dispatch as cited by the hon. member is certainly inaccurate. Consideration is being given to various proposals for preliminary discussions among the members of the commonwealth on the Japanese peace settlement, but no final decision has yet been taken in regard to any of these proposals. At a convenient time I propose to make a fuller statement of the attitude being taken by this government in respect of the Japanese peace settlement.

subtopic: JAPANESE PEACE SETTLEMENT-PRESS REPORT FROM LONDON
speechtext:
If I may ask a supplemental question, is the minister in a position yet to say whether or not the reports that the conference will be an eleven-power conference are correct? Apparently the thought is that the eleven nations who fought against Japan would be represented in the conference.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I cannot say that any determination has been made in that regard. The foreign secretary of the United Kingdom stated recently at Margate that it was his view that these eleven powers should be associated in the preparation of the treaty, and that is a view that is shared by the Canadian government.

VETERANS* PREFERENCE-INQUIRY AS TO PROCEDURE IN CASE OF ERROR
On the orders of the day:
Mr. LESLIE A. MUTCH (Winnipeg South): I wish to direct a question to the Secretary of State, of which I have given him notice. Has the civil service commission, having assigned to a position in the civil

service a veteran who is not entitled to the veterans' preference, the right to require his dismissal in spite of the fact that he has accepted the position in good faith and performed his duties satisfactorily, when they subsequently discover that he should not in the first instance have been accorded the veterans' preference?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg South was good enough to send me notice of his question. I am informed that the general policy of the civil service commission is that where an error has been made owing to a mistake on the part of the commission, the veteran is not penalized; but where there has been an error owing to a misstatement or wrong information given by the veteran himself, he must assume the responsibility. If the hon. member wishes to give me information concerning any individual case, I shall be very happy to have it investigated.

I have a question which I should like to put to the Minister of Finance with reference to this third resolution. In putting it I am bearing in mind that the resolution is stated in general terms, and the question is one of interpretation. What
appears in the resolution is that the rates for the year will be the average of the present rates for the first half of the year and the new rates for the second half. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The answer is yes. As the resolution indicates, the rates in effect for 1947 will be the arithmetical average of the rates existing up to July 1 and the new rates. For example, the rate for the first half of 1947 in the low bracket is 22 per cent. The new starting rate is 10 per cent. The sum of those is 32, and the arithmetical average is 16. The tax payable in the case cited by my hon. friend will be at the appropriate rate for the full year. The bill when it is brought in will contain a special schedule setting forth the effective rate for 1947, which will be a schedule made up of the average of the two rates to which I have just referred.

Then in any case where death has taken place and a T.l return has already been filed by the executor on behalf of the deceased in respect of 1947 income, steps should be taken now to revise the return?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To revise the return and obtain the appropriate refund, if one is due. That is correct.

I should like to say a word or two about taxation in connection with teacher's contributions to the superannuation fund, based upon a letter which arrived just in time to be discussed on this resolution. The system of pension for teachers in Saskatchewan has been based on a double or triple scheme. It is partly a service pension and partly made up of the proceeds of whatever annuity certain contributions made throughout the teacher's earning life will buy. Up to the present, under the Saskatchewan Teachers' Superannuation Act of 1942, the amount of statutory deduction has been four per cent. To that act there has been an amendment by which the teacher is now allowed to pay in, in addition to his compulsory four per cent, certain payments which I suppose might be classed as voluntary. They are voluntary in regard to paying in
Income War Tax Act

but they are not voluntary in regard to taking out, because I understand that the amendment sees to it that the funds are kept in there until the teacher ceases to teach. It is the desire of the Saskatchewan teachers' federation, as expressed in this letter from the secretary, that this matter be brought to the attention of the minister for the purpose of discovering the position in regard to these extra payments. I might read a line or two from the letter:
This year's amendment to the act-
That is the Saskatchewan Teachers' Superannuation Act of 1942.
- provides that not less than four per cent shall be deducted at the source but a teacher may elect to have a greater percentage deducted at source, and we are asking that any amount deducted be exempt from income tax.
My correspondents point out that the dominion act provides for exemptions up to an amount of $900 per annum. They also point out that if a teacher contributes to the fund and1 withdraws those contributions, that amount is taxable as income for the year in which it is withdrawn. That is to say, under the new policy, which I think was initiated m 1945, if pensions are liable to income tax then contributions should not be; otherwise you have a system of double taxation. Perhaps the minister would comment on that. In the meantime, in Hansard for 1945, at page 3427, I found something said by the previous minister of finance on this matter:
We are now changing the law in accordance with the recommendations of the royal commission to make all contributions to the pension plan deductible from income for tax purposes and to provide in general that pension payments shall be subject to tax.
That was where I got this idea of double taxation. On the previous page the former minister is reported to have said:
In the future it will not be possible to set up funds like that at all. The income of the fund will be free of tax, but the pensioner, the contributor, in every case will be entitled to deduct his contributions from his income for tax purposes and he will be taxed in full on his pension.
Perhaps the minister would comment on that so we can get some guidance for these people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is correct. Polio wing the Ives commission report the law was amended to provide that payments to a pension fund could be deducted from the income of the person paying, for income tax purposes, but that the income payments when received would be taxed. That of course is subject to the general qualification in the act that the 
fund must be one that is approved by the Minister of National Revenue as being a pension fund eligible under the act. I am not familiar with the Saskatchewan statute or the practice to which the hon. gentleman refers, but I suggest that if there is any doubt as to the application of the statute the matter should be submitted to the deputy minister of national revenue for a ruling. I think the hon. gentleman will find that the matter can be best dealt with in that way.

Just along the same line may I ask the minister to state the present position with regard to the pension, for example, paid by the C.P.R. to an employee who has retired? I have had a communication from one who has been on pension for nine or ten years, and who is being charged income tax on that pension. Is there no protection in a case of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am advised that up to 1935 the C.P.R. pension fund was non-contributory, and of course in that case the total pension would be subject to tax when received by the pensioner. In 1935 it was converted to a contributory fund, and since that time employees of the C.P.R. have been making contributions. I am told the Department of National Revenue now apportions the pension payments received by C.P.R. pensioners as between the portion which was non-contributory and the portion which was contributory, and makes a- proper tax adjustment.
In other words if the man retired in 1934 his whole pension would be taxable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.
Does not the minister think some adjustment should be made to meet that situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I don't know why. It is a non-contributory plan; it is a free gift, and following the ordinary rule it is subject to tax when received. There has been no double taxation in that case, of course. The purpose of the law as it now stands, following the recommendations of the Ives commission, is that it should be so arranged that there will not be double taxation on these pensions. The general rule is that if the pension contribution may be taken as a deduction from income for tax purposes when it is paid in, then the pension is taxable; and that is the provision as it now stands.

Is not the actual position this, that the man was receiving a certain rate of pay which, while it may not have been

Income War Tax Act
apportioned in such a way that part of it was shown to be a contribution to a pension fund, nevertheless probably was based on the fact that he was going to get a pension upon retirement? Surely some relief could be given these elderly men who are in that category.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course the short answer to my hon. friend's question is that if he had received his pension contribution as part of his pay, he would have paid tax on it. In fact he did not. Reasoning it in logic, he received pay on which he paid tax at the proper rate. If for the purposes of argument we say that in addition the company was paying into a pension fund a certain amount of money to provide him with a pension later, then that was something he was getting free of income tax, something which was not included in his income for purposes of taxation. Therefore following the rule I have just mentioned, when his pension is received it should be subject to tax.
Yes, but even on that basis his increased income would have been very much smaller. It would not be right to tax him on his full pension, which is what is happening today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Generally speaking I think it is more favourable to the taxpayer, certainly under existing rates of tax, to deduct his pension contributions for purposes of income tax, than to have a tax-free pension at the end, because the pension, except in the executive groups, is relatively small and usually covered by the exemption, so the pensioner pays very little tax. Taxwise I think it is very much in the interests of the pensioner to claim the pension contributions as a deduction from income when he is earning at a fairly high rate and is subject to a fairly substantial tax, than to have a tax free pension. I am informed it works out that way.

I quite agree with the minister, but all these men now would be well over seventy-five. They retire at sixty-five, and having retired before 1935 they are getting on in years. I would ask that consideration be given to providing some relief for men in that position.
Just before eleven o'clock on Wednesday evening I asked the minister a number of questions in connection with farmers' income tax. I wonder if he has the answers for me today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I assured my hon. friend that I would get the information and give it to him. It requires a bit of time; I may not
be able to do so while we are on the resolutions, but I repeat the assurance, which I think was the one I gave the other night, that at the latest I will give it when we are in committee on the appropriate section of the bill. It has not been overlooked.

I wish to draw to the attention of the minister a matter somewhat similar to that which was brought forward by my colleague to my left a few moments ago. I want to recall the change made in the law last year under resolution 27 at that time, which is carried into the present consolidation of the act in clause 9, paragraph 7. Under that provision, in the case of payments pursuant to superannuation or pension fund or upon retirement, as the law stood immediately preceding last July such a payment was taxable spread over five years, one-fifth each year. This paragraph 7, as it stands, made the tax fall very much more heavily, although there is one alternative, because it is taxable in the year it is received. I want to suggest to the minister two things, first of all that that contravenes substantially what was suggested or recommended in the Ives report, and secondly that it creates a great hardship, particularly in the case of widows.
I want to read a brief statement here- I believe it is correct-which sets out a case of great hardship which I would bring to the minister's attention. It states:
At the last session of parliament the government had changes made in regard to the methods of taxation of "lump sum" payments from pension funds and employer's gratuities to those retiring from service. When the matter was discussed in the house by the ways and means committee as reported at pages 3871 to 3876 of Hansard, Mr. Abbott, who was piloting the matter through, stated that the method then in vogue, i.e., taxation of only one-third of the lump sum, was "introduced during the war to moderate the effect of very high tax rates," and throughout his defence of the proposed change to revert to the system of taxing the whole of those payments, implied that taxation was now lower. This debate took place in July, 1946 . . . As Hansard will show, Mr. Abbott spoke only of men receiving lump sum payments during their lifetime; he did not make clear that this also affected widows, or other beneficiaries of a person who had made payments into pension funds and that as a rule the lump sum consisted entirely of the man's own payment into the fund.
And then this further:
Prior to 4942, or thereabout, the taxation on lump sum repayments from pension funds was on the full amount. As the result of representations made by various organizations, among which was the international firefighters' union, the tax was reduced to one-third. When the Ives commission was set up the organization referred to appeared before them in regard to "lump sum" taxation.
Income War Tax Act

The organization referred to was the international fire fighters' union, I might say.
The commission, in its report-
That is the Ives commission-
-commented on the difficulties surrounding the question and recommend the continuation of the one-third as being equitable. On page 3871 of Hansard, during the discussion on resolution No. 26, Mr. Abbott said: "The whole question was considered by the Ives commission and legislation was introduced last year following the recommendations of that commission."
I would submit that this finding of the Ives commission was not followed throughout, and in this particular it was disregarded.
I should like to bring one case to the attention of the minister:, and then I shall have finished. This is a case respecting one of the members of the fire fighters' union in Toronto. It states:
One of their members, after nearly thirty years of service retired on pension; he died within a few months; his widow received as a lump sum repayment of his contributions to the pension fund about $3,200. Under the present regulations she has two choices in regard to the tax. One would mean, in round figures, a tax of $500 out of the $3,200; the other a tax of $780. But here's "the rub,"-this man during the first half of his service on account of income, was not taxable. It was only when his wages got higher and his family grew up, and more particularly when the government dipped much lower than formerly into low and medium incomes, that he became taxable and was exempted from such tax on the amounts he was then paying into his pension fund. As a result of these exemptions he saved $209. Now, owing to the taxation being on the whole $3,200, his widow received, and which amount represented all his payments into the fund, even those in the years when he was not taxable, his widow has to nay either $500 or $780.
I just wish to recapitulate at this point. It seems to me that the change which was made last year and which, I submit, made taxation on such payments so much mote onerous, was a most unfortunate one. I hope the minister will be able to take this situation into consideration, and particularly as it affects widows.
And I just add this: I was informed-and this may be subject to correction-that actually a regulation has been made easing these cases where widows are affected. I should like to know if that is so. If it is so I would ask two questions: first, under what authority does that come, and, second, if it is proper to do it there, why should not the principle be extended?
I repeat that it seems to me the amount of the tax involved is, at any rate in the smaller cases, negligible so far as the crown is concerned, and a very great hardship can be and is being worked in many cases similar to the one I have just brought to the attention of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This question, as my hon. friend knows, is complicated. It is one which has been given a good deal of consideration by myself and by the officers of my department for the last three or four months. I have had a number of delegations to see me about it.
It is true that the law as it stands did depart in certain respects from the recommendations of the Ives report. That was done, I believe, for good and sufficient reasons. These lump sum payments can be made the subject of considerable abuse. And when I state that I am dealing with the general aspect of the problem, rather than with the specific case to which the hon. member referred. But I repeat that they can be made the subject of abuse. A man can accumulate a certain amount, and then leave the company he is with, get his payments, go to another company and get another lump sum payment.
Broadly speaking-and I think this is a view which is shared by many people-I believe that a pension plan which provides for single lump sum payments to widows is not a particularly good plan. As I say, I am only expressing my own personal view. I think it is a much-better plan if the directors of the fund are given the option of paying the amount to the widow in yearly instalments. I advised some of these delegations, which came to see me and which discussed certain funds, that the department would have no objection to a fund amending its by-laws or regulations, or whatever they may be, to make the provision I have indicated; and, in addition, to provide that it could be or should be paid in instalments. I went further and said that the department would be prepared to look at hardship cases where a lump sum payment should be made-for instance in order to pay off a pressing mortgage obligation. I said the department would be prepared to look at those cases involving a particular remission under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act.
I feel that that is really as far as we should go in that field. However it is a question on which I have a perfectly open mind; and if it can be shown that another scheme might be fairer and better, we would be prepared to consider it. But this is a matter which has been given a great deal of careful consideration by myself-and I am not an expert in it-and also by departmental officials who are informed in these matters. It has been considered sympathetically, too, I may add.

I agree it is unfortunate that this condition exists with respect to lump sum payments, and I agree with the minister's view that it would be wise to adopt a different course.

Income War Tax Act
There are one or two respects in which I differ from the minister. I have no doubt there may be cases where people go from one place to another and may accumulate pensions -although I would think, and I suggest with deference to the minister, that the type of men who roll about are not the ones who are likely to accumulate much by way of pension. I should not consider that a very serious point. It is one which it seems to me could be taken care of by a suitable safeguard. Further, I deprecate the idea that we have to meet a situation of this kind, which I assume is a situation which will arise often, practically by charitable considerations. Perhaps I should withdraw the word "charitable" and say it is unfortunate that we must meet it by making special cases. It is most undesirable, first of all because people do not want to be a subject of charity; secondly because they do not know what their rights are, and thirdly because to some extent it depends on whether the minister had a good night's sleep. The minister being human, it depends upon that.
Is he human?

I am giving the minister the benefit of the doubt. But I do come back to this, that I do not have to remind the minister that a year ago we departed radically from what the situation has been before. And looking back upon the debates which took place at that time, I must reproach those of us on this side of the house for not' fighting it with more strength.
We departed radically because, as was pointed out in the Ives report, broadly speaking there was a practice-which as the report says was not logical, but which seemed to have common sense in it-of spreading payment out over five years. The report says that under the circumstances there seems to be no particular reason for changing the existing law. I must say that on general principle it does seem to me to be sensible. We have done jt in various cases. When you get a lump sum payment of this kind I think it should be spread over some years. I think that carries with it the judgment of everybody as being just a matter of common sense. If there are difficulties in the way, that is a matter for the minister and his advisers. It may be, although I am not suggesting this particularly, that the minister and his advisers feel that this has to be limited to sums of modest amounts. I am not offering an opinion on that, but I do suggest most earnestly that what we did last year w'as a reactionary move. The case that I have given shows the 83166-231

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The total amount of the revenue, of course.. In increasing the exemption I think that $8 out of $10 would go to those in the upper brackets. The effect would be that they would benefit by raising the exemptions. I suppose that approximately $50 or $60 million in tax would be lost by increasing the exemptions for single persons to $1,000 and married persons to $2,000. If one took into account only the loss of revenue from people in these brackets, what would be the result? You would give no reduction to the man who earns $2,001 or $2,500. You would have to start increasing the tax. In other words you have to increase the rates of tax on everybody above $2,000 to the extent of say $50 million; and the practice in other countries where income tax has been highly developed, including Great Britain which is under a socialist government today, and Australia which is under a socialist government, and New Zealand which is under a socialist government, shows that the exemptions are lower than they are in Canada. I feel strongly that the income tax level is fair, eminently fair, just as fair as if not fairer than the level in other advanced countries. I say that to increase the exemptions will create more unfairness rather than less. To use a slang phrase, I am convinced that this plea for increasing income tax exemptions is a phony in so far as it will benefit the vast majority of the people of the country who have to pay taxes. I do not suggest that the hon. gentlemen who put it forward believe that for one moment. I do not impute motives. I know they genuinely believe that it is in the interest of the lower income levels. But my contention is that it is not. I think there is a point beyond which you hurt them rather than help them, because of the fact I mentioned in the budget speech that, rightly or wrongly, or any way you put it, half the people who earn income are below the existing level. There is no use. fooling ourselves. This tax revenue has to be got somewhere, and it cannot all be got from people of any figure you like, $5,000 a year and up, if you like, because there are simply not enough of them in the country to do it. If therefore we do not have a well worked out, well adjusted income tax schedule, we shall have to get the revenue some other

way, and that means indirect taxes, which work much more injustice on the low income groups than on the high.
That is my view and I hold it strongly. I am a strong believer in a well thought out, graduated, progressive income tax scheme, and that is what I believe we have in this country today. I believe that in fairness income tax relief should be graduated in all groups in the community, naturally less for those with high incomes. But the method suggested of raising the exemptions would not in my judgment accomplish the purpose intended.

I do not see how the minister can argue that by raising the exemptions you do not benefit the majority, because the figures I have show that if you increase the exemptions for married people to $2,000 and single people to $1,200 you relieve 54 per cent of the taxpayers. In other words, the majority would benefit, and not the minority, by such action.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The majority would benefit by unduly penalizing the minority. That is the fact. No man can convince me that the man with $2,500 or $3,000 or $3,500 is not entitled to just as much consideration, on a logical and reasonable basis, in the matter of tax treatment under the income tax act, or under any other act, as the man earning $1,500 or $1,800. It is true that taxes should be imposed in proportion to ability to pay, but you do not do that by an arbitrary exemption. I repeat what I said before. If the argument from analogy is of value, we are not doing too badly when our exemption levels are higher than those in any other country.
But it wrnuld be a good thing for this country to take the lead.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have taken the lead in many things, and we have done so in this instance.

There is no reason why we should not continue. If you raised the exemptions to $1,200 for single and $2,000 for married persons, from the figures I have obtained, on the basis of 1945, it would cost the government a loss of revenue of $98 million, not taking into consideration the amount lost in respect of people above the proposed exemptions. But in view of the fact that we are bringing about a reduction of revenue greater than $98 million, we could increase the exemptions and at the same time allow for a reduction in revenue from people in the lower income brackets above S2.000 and $1,200.

the Alberta farmer? union. I refer to No. 7 on the list, which asks that payment of arrears of interest and principal on farm loans due in 1940 be allowed as deductions for income tax purposes. That is from the farmers union, which is almost identical with the one from the federation of agriculture, which asks that payment of arrears of interest and principal on farms due for 1940 be allowed as deductions for income tax purposes. I feel there is every justification for that demand. It is true that last year we introduced legislation to make it possible for the farmer to average his income over a period of three years. The majority of farmer members last year took the stand that the period should be increased to five, but there was a compromise on three years. That, however, was not made retroactive and therefore we find today that many farmers are having to pay tax on debts that were incurred in the past, and therefore the federation of agriculture and the farmers union ask that where payments are made on certain debts incurred in the past, no income tax be charged thereon. There is every justification for that position, for this reason. In the thirties the farmers, through no fault of their own, were forced into debt owing to the fact that they were having to produce at considerably below the cost of production. That was due to the policy of the government of the day.
At that time the farmers were told that they would have to accept world market prices, and that situation continued until 1942, and the farmers kept going into debt. Then in 1942 prices of agricultural products were increased, but at the same time the income tax was greatly increased. Moreover, it might have been possible for the farmers to get higher prices, but the government placed a ceiling on agricultural prices. The result was that we found ourselves faced with this situation. In peace time when prices were low the farmers were told they would have to accept world prices, and when the war came and prices went up they were not allowed to get the advantage of world prices but were told that they would have to take less. Nevertheless they were faced with the problem of having to meet debts that had been incurred in the period of low prices, and those debts unquestionably represent to a large extent unpaid expenditures.
Expenditures incurred in production should be allowed as cost and therefore deductible from taxation. But today, when the farmer tries to meet obligations incurred in the thirties, he finds that those obligations are increased to from 30 to 40 per cent as a result of having to pay income tax. I think the suggestion of the federation of agriculture is reasonable, that repayment of interest and capital on mortgages incurred prior to 1940 should be exempt from taxation.
There is nothing new in this principle. We have adopted it in regard to certain other corporations in the country, and if we can adopt it so far as those corporations are concerned, I cannot see why the principle cannot be followed in agriculture. Agriculture is probably one of the most risky occupations in the country. We have to realize, therefore, that although it is doing fairly well today it may run up against very great difficulties in the future-not as serious, we hope, as in the thirties; nevertheless we may run into a situation where it may be impossible for the farmer to recover cost of production in the prices he receives, and hence he will run into debt once more.
I suggest it would be a good thing if we were to allow the farmers to establish a reserve fund to offset future losses. We must help them not only to get out of debt but to establish such a reserve to take care of future losses. We do that in connection with the chartered banks. We allow them to set aside a certain amount as reserve; the public are not allowed to know what that inner reserve is, and the banks pay no income tax on the amount they put in that reserve. When they suffer losses they can draw money from such reserves to meet' those losses, and the excuse given is that these losses are unpaid expenditures and therefore should not be taxed.
I contend that exactly the same principle should be applied to farmers. They should be allowed to meet losses which represent expenditures without having to pay income tax on them. The chartered banks have always argued that inner reserves are merely for the purpose of meeting losses, and they emphasize the fact that during the thirties they suffered heavy losses and had to use up a large percentage of those reserves. But I think it is more true to say that the inner reserves are not merely for the purpose of meeting possible losses but for the purpose of guaranteeing profits, because during the thirties the chartered banks averaged dividends of around nine or ten per cent on paid-up capital. I do not see therefore how you can Say that they were having heavy losses when they were able to pay around nine or ten per cent dividends. The fact that they could pay such dividends proves that they were using inner reserves to guarantee profits; and yet they were not charged income tax on the reserves because it is claimed that those reserves were for the purpose of meeting losses. Apparently we are still continuing that policy. In 1943,

to ameliorate such conditions and to remove anomalies which have resulted from the strict application of the law.

I should like to add my words to those of other hon. members who have spoken in regard to this matter of farm income tax. We have been discussing these matters in the house for a number of years now; since 1944 we have been raising these questions of the basic herd, in regard to reserves, in regard to what deductions should be allowed in respect to interest, and various other matters. I believe we are making some progress, but we have still a long way to go before we give the farmer the same deal that is enjoyed by other groups in our economy.
I agree with the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Acadia, and there is one particular point I want to bring to the attention of the minister. That is the matter of allowing payments of interest as a deduction. During the thirties, in a great many cases in Saskatchewan and the other western provinces, and in fact all across Canada, people got behind with the interest on their mortgages. In 1937, 1938, 1939 and 1940 various agreements were reached with the mortgage companies whereby the mortgages were consolidated.	In some cases the companies
reduced the amount of interest due and then had a new agreement drawn up under which the remaining interest became part of the principal and the new agreement took effect as from that date. Now when a farmer makes a payment on that principal he is not allowed to deduct that portion which really represented interest and was consolidated with the principal. A farmer may have borrowed money at the bank. He may have had a crop failure; there may have been grasshoppers or something else may have happened so that he was not able to meet the note. He went to the bank and the manager said, "Well, we will just include that interest with the principal in a new note," and the new note is made out. The farmer is allowed to deduct the interest paid on the new note, but he is not allowed to deduct that part of the payments on the note represented by interest, and I think the government should give some consideration to that matter. I believe that where there has been a consolidation of a loan, the amount of that consolidation representing interest should be deductible with respect to income tax. I do not know to just what extent that is being done, but I feel that it could be done by regulation rather than by a change in the act, and I ask the minister to give consideration to this suggestion.
I would say also that there should be some uniformity in the administration of the income

tax as between various districts in the country. I answered the hon. member for Cariboo a few minutes ago by saying that my view is that the determination of that question is not one which requires legislation, and that the question as to what is capital and what is income in respect of a farmer who sells his herd of cattle is one for administrative determination under the provision of the act as it stands.
I understand that some relief has been afforded in respect of dispersal sales-whatever those may be. Perhaps the term is more or less self-explanatory. However I am informed -and I believe my information is correct-that no amendment to the law is required to enable the Department of National Revenue to determine, in respect of the sale of a herd, what portion of the purchase price is capital and what portion is income. I should think that if a taxpayer feels he is aggrieved by the decision of the taxing authority, he should then lodge an appeal, because it is really a question of fact, pure and simple, and is based upon recognized accounting principles. As I see it, the only way to cure it would be to enact some specific provision of law which would depart from recognized accounting principles.

I should like to say a word or two at this point. I had intended rising before the minister, but I was too slow. The way I see the picture is this. Let us assume there are two men, one of whom bought a half section of land for which, we will say, he paid $2,000. Then his friend bought $2,000 worth of cattle, and grazed them on the first man's half section. The man who bought the cattle works hard and, before the years of heavy income tax, we will say he increased the value of his herd to $5,000, or to the point where he owns $5,000 worth of cattle. In the meantime, the value of the land has increased. These men put up the same amount of money, but one worked hard and the other did no work. The value of the man's land increased to $5,000, representing a capital gain of $3,000, and he pays no tax. The other man, who put up the same amount of money to buy cattle, and who worked hard with the herd, pays on the total increase.
Then the man who did the work becomes ill, or dies, and a sale must be made. In that event the tax is paid on the total increased value of the herd. On the other hand, the man who bought land has to pay nothing at all by way of taxation.
Do not misunderstand me. I realize fully the difficulties which confront one when he attempts to deal with this question. I fully

362S
Income War Tax Act

realize that no one should be permitted to buy a couple of cows and let them increase until disposal time without paying any income tax. He has not paid any income tax because, owing to the fact that he has not sold any, he has had no income. Of course, if the minister were a stock man we would know that he would have to get rid of a bull or two, because they have to be changed now and again.
In the hypothetical case I have given, I can see that there might be some evasion; and I do not mean that it would be deliberate. However, there might be some injustice so far as the taxing authority is concerned. But I assure the minister of this, that in that ranching and farming country in which I live this is the greatest source of irritation.
As a suggestion, I do not see why the Department of National Revenue, the collecting department, cannot do something like this. Generally speaking, those men do not keep books. The big fellows do, but the intermediate and smaller men do not. I do not see why it could not be found, as a question of fact, what a man's herd was at a given date To use a word which is disliked, it could be done in an arbitrary fashion. Choose an arbitrary date, and put it on a basis that people can understand.
I should like to say one thing more; and in this instance I have a file from which to get the facts. The same principle is involved. My inquiry comes from a public administrator in the judicial district of Calgary in the province of Alberta. I have had correspondence with Mr. Brown, who is no longer there, and with Mr. McAdams. The correspondence is not complete, because, unfortunately, they lost the file which contained my original correspondence. I am not blaming anybody for that; I have lost files myself. Those things happen.
This man is a public administrator, and in an estate which he administers he has some producers' certificates, which are received from the sale of grain. The Minister of Trade and Commerce will understand that. They are treating those certificates as being both capital and income. I think that should be rectified immediately. What I am referring to is going on at the present time. It may be a mere incident; perhaps there are not many people *who die and who have producers' certificates, but the thing is utterly wrong. Will the Minister of National Revenue please not think I am blaming any one in his department for losing a few' letters. I am more likely to lose letters than he is.
To come back to this herd business and matters of that kind, these things are not only serious to the individual; they are most

irritating, broadly speaking. It seems to me that a great improvement could be made in that subdivision or area of taxation of farmers or cattle raisers.

The minister asked for a definition of basic and herd and I should like to give him one as understood by the average farmer. A farmer may have been going on from year to year without being eligible for income tax. He will have built up his herd. Then in 1944 he reaches a point where he is taxable on his income. He has at that time thirty head of cattle, the herd having been built up when he was not taxable. Then in 1946 when he has increased this herd to forty he sells everything. He is then taxable on the whole forty instead of just the ten he has accumulated since becoming eligible for income tax. I think that is the idea which the average farmer has in mind.
The federation of agriculture has a similar idea, but instead of doing it on an individual basis they take the year 1941 as being the year in which a number of farmers came under the income tax and they ask that the year 1941 be used as a basis. The department could use either method, but I think most people would prefer the individual basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am interested in my hon. friend's definition of basic herd. All I can say offhand is that it would change the size of the basic herd with the increased income tax exemption or because of the number of children a man might have.

In spite of the minister's last remark, I still agree with those who have spoken. I am in favour of having some basis for establishing basic herds for the taxation of farmers. The other evening the hon. member for Battle River asked some questions and the minister promised to give replies. Before he does so, I should like to say a word or two about one of the things mentioned in the united farmers and the farmers' union brief, so that the minister may make provision for this when he brings in his bill.
It may not seem important to many people when I mention the digging of wells, but I would point out to the minister and to the committee that a well on a farm is of almost paramount importance. In many of the branch offices no allowance is made for deducting the cost of digging a well. Whether that is a principle adopted by the revenue department or w'hether it is a matter of administration, I do not know. I can quite understand that if a farmer were to dig a well costing $1,000 and got water, he would not be entitled to deduct the total cost of the well but he could depreciate it over a period.

Income War Tax Act
But a farmer who is anxious to obtain water may dig four or five wells costing anywhere from S400 to SI.000 and sometimes S2.000 each, and yet strike no water. Such a man would not have improved his capital position. In fact he has depleted his income and his capital position, and no provision is made for that. That happens quite frequently. When it comes to the matter of exploring for petroleum a different method is used. Petroleum companies are allowed to deduct for income tax purposes a certain percentage of the amounts expended for exploration purposes, and dry wells come under that regulation. I am not complaining about that but I do say.that the exploring for petroleum is no more important to those companies or to the people of the country than is the digging for water to a farmer. If it is fair to allow these deductions in connection with petroleum explorations, the same principle should be applied to farmers who are digging wells.
Many other points were mentioned in the brief of the farmers' union and the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, but they have been dealt with and I shall confine my presentation to this matter of digging wrells which is so important to the farmers of this country.

While the time may come in the future when every one will fill out his income tax form with a great deal of pleasure, nevertheless the case cited by the hon. member for Calgary West is one of those things that irritate people, and the more irritation and inequality we can remove, the better it will be for all. I rise to mention one matter in connection with people doing w'ork for government departments on behalf of the farmers.
A veterinary surgeon doing work for the Department of Agriculture is allowed nine cents a mile for driving his car. A rate of nine cents is not outrageous for driving through country districts. There is one veterinary in my district who sometimes covers 2,000 miles in a month and he will work six months in the year for the department. When it comes to making out their income tax returns these men are told that they will not be allowed nine cents a mile for expenses, that the allowance will be limited to four and a half cents a mile and that twenty-five per cent will be taken off the luxury driving.
Generally speaking, a man who drives 2,000 miles a month or 18.000 miles in six months on behalf of the Department of Agriculture is not going to do much luxury driving. I just want to draw the minister's attention to 83166-232i
this thing which is so irritating. If the Department of Agriculture allows nine cents and that is a fair price-why should the income tax division not also allow nine cents. This thing has been going on for a long time and I am drawing it to the attention of the minister in the hope that it will be corrected.

May I add one further word which I think will be helpful. We are really talking about cows. A man will have so much land which will maintain a certain number of cattle, and the number generally remains fairly stationary. If a cow becomes too old, he may sell it but he replaces it with another one. Let us take 1941 as the base period, assuming that that has been fixed. A man has fort}' cows worth $100 apiece. We will assume that in 1945 he still has forty cows, but they are now worth $150 apiece. We all know that cattle have advanced considerably. By 1945 the man has had a capital gain of fifty per cent.
If I bought land or stocks or shares or some machinery and sell it at an increased price, that is not taxable as income. The farmer with his forty head of cattle who sells them at an increase of fifty per cent, has had a capital gain just as surely as in the case of these other sales. Yet he is assessed with the sale price as income today.
Mr. GI'LLIS: I would not rise except for a definition which the minister placed upon the question raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South, namely, that of exempting pensions for income tax purposes. In reply to the hon. member, the minister said that these pensions, voluntary or contributory, were somewhat of a gift.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; I was referring only to non-contributory pensions.

One could classify the others as almost seventy-five per cent gift, because they' are all three-way pensions. I want to put the minister right at the start. None of these things is a gift, because if one contributes to a pension on a voluntary basis or otherwise, the first charge on his wages in the negotiations is that gift.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree that the word "gift'' should be changed.
He might have been receiving ten per cent or fifteen per cent more in wages w'ere it not for the fact that a retiring allowance was established.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my' hon. friend will allow me. the reason I made the remark was that if he had received fifteen per cent extra on wages he would have paid taxes on it.

The minister might well consider exempting pensions for income tax purposes. If you calculate the amount I believe the government would lose very little money if they did not collect taxes from pensioners. Few pensioners are in the income tax brackets. Nevertheless there are a few, and we hope some time to raise the pensions above the exemption levels. We are trying to take time by the forelock and get ahead of the minister.
There is another pension or retiring allowance which, in my opinion, is treated rather badly. Take a civil servant who has contributed to a superannuation fund for fifteen or twenty years. There were some of them in the service who during the past war joined the armed forces. They withdrew their superannuation allowance in the form of a lump sum, and they were taxed on the lump sum payment, despite the fact that it was paid in over a period of fifteen or twenty years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that they were taxed only on one-third of the amount.
I do not know; my information is that they were assessed on the whole amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: After the war rates came in, I am informed that they were assessed only on one-third.

The minister might check that. It was wrong to do it in the way in which it was done. Many of these young fellows came back to the service but could not return to their old positions. They took a lower position, and I believe that the payment should have been considered as a gift; there should have been no assessment against the superannuation. A man builds it up over a period of fifteen or twenty years with the expectation that it will carry him over the lean years of his life. He becomes patriotic and joins the services, offers his life to his country, and what he has built up to care for his old age is taxed. When he comes back he takes a lower position with no expectancy of comfort if and when he reaches the age where that is necessary.
These are the two points that I wish to mention. Because of the small amount of revenue that the department would be losing in taxes, the minister should make an announcement as soon as possible to the effect that in future pensioners of this country will be tax free.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am always tremendously struck with the voluntary assistance I receive in methods of reducing revenue and increasing expenditures, but I get few suggestions for

increasing revenue. Of course, as hon. members know, my problem is to make ends meet if possible, so that I cannot-much as my heart is touched by a good many of these appeals-accede to them all.
- Mr. KNOWLES: In answering certain arguments put forward by this side of the house, a while ago the minister used the word "phony". I realize that he was in a pleasant mood when he used it and had a smile on his face, but I fear it was-

-raising the exemption levels. The minister said that it was the responsibility of the government to be fair to all members of society, and that consideration had to be given to the $3,500 man and the $5,000 man as well as to those in the $1,500 and $2,000 brackets. May I say to the minister that if he thinks there is anything phony and fallacious about the argument from this side of the house, then his argument fails to take into consideration all the facts of the matter. What one has to consider in these' matters is not just the amount that is being paid by taxpayers, but the amount that they have left. According to the new rates, after the $2,000 man pays his taxes he will have $1,930 left in 1948; that is in the case of a married man. The $5,000 married taxpayer will have $4,330 left after he pays taxes, and the $200,000 married taxpayer will have $67,507 left. There are all the gradations in between. I suggest that the responsibility of government, yes, is to all its citizens, to the whole community, but its responsibility is greater to those in the lower income brackets than it is to those further up.
The minister just said that it is his problem to try to make ends meet. I suggest that it is also the responsibility of the government to tiy to help the people to make ends meet. Those who are down in the brackets of $1,500 to $2,000 simply cannot do it, let alone the thousands of people who are even below these levels, and therefore are not liable to pay taxes at all.	.
It seems to me that in the whole of this discussion about income tax, revenues and expenditures of the government, the government's approach is too much of a business one and not a human one. The government

Income War Tax Act
seems to think its job is simply to get such revenues as it can to discharge governmental responsibilities at a minimum. We feel that the budget of a country should be such as to provide for the welfare of all the citizens.
The minister has just said that he gets few suggestions as to how to increase revenue. My desk-mate, the hon. member for Mackenzie, will continue with the reply that I am making to the minister's statement of a while back and offer him a suggestion or two.
Before I take my seat I should like to ask the minister one other question about another subject on which I hope he will make a statement before this item passes. My other question has to do with refundable savings that were taken during certain years of the war. I know the act provides that the first of these savings shall be repaid not later than March 31, 1948, and then there is a sort of revolving-door policy from there on. But it also provides that ' the governor in council may make payments at an earlier day.
As the minister knows, there are people who, during the war years, were in the income brackets and were paying these refundable savings, who are now in straitened circumstances. A great many feel that some provision should be made to pay these savings back to them now, when they are needed. It would be desirable if the minister could make some statement as to the plans of the government in connection with this matter. Is there any chance of the first payment being made earlier than was anticipated? Also, when payments start, are they to be spread over a period of years, or is there some chance that people in straitened circumstances may be able to get back at once all that is coming to them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
At the moment I cannot go farther than I stated before, namely, that, in accordance with the statute, refundable payments due by March 31 next will be paid by that time. This involves the sending out of several hundred thousand cheques and there is much mechanical and administrative work there. What it may be possible to do in future years with respect to accelerating payments, or possibly attempting to do something about payment on a selective basis in cases of hardship, is a question regarding which I cannot make a statement at the moment. There are tremendous difficulties in the way of making a selective refund of these refundable portions. One who reads the mail on it is struck, of course, by cases in which genuine need is demonstrated; but naturally, human nature being what it is, if refunds were made in anticipation on a selective basis, many people would apply who would not, strictly
speaking, be entitled to get it, and this would mean that every case would have to be investigated. Briefly, I am not prepared to make a statement as to what the government might be able to do, other than the one I have already given, that this year's contractual obligation will be met, and we shall have to see later whether something can be done.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The other matter is still being studied?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That and other things like it are being continually studied.

As I followed the minister's remarks, I made a few rapid calculations as the debate proceeded. I anticipated that he would want information to indicate what might be done if the income tax brackets were raised. In answer to a question of mine the other night, the minister intimated that if all income tax payers receiving less than $1,000 for unmarried persons and less than $2,000 for married were exempt, it would mean a loss of revenue of $200 million, and those who are critical of government policy might fairly be expected to make some suggestions.
I think it is a sound principle of taxation that in a country as rich as Canada we should have a minimum below which no citizen should be expected to live. The Minister of Justice sets standards for people in the penitentiaries. It is a credit to Canada that we should provide medical services, dental services, adequate food and heated accommodation for criminals. I suggest that it is equally desirable that all citizens should have a minimum below which they should not have to live, and likewise we should have a maximum so that there would be a ceiling on incomes. I would not expect the Minister of Finance to advance this, but I think all members would agree with me that the Minister of Finance should possibly have one of the highest salaries in the dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.

Perhaps we should say that the highest income should go to the Prime Minister. That would be only fair The one selected by the people to hold the most important position should have the highest income that we are prepared to leave to any one individual. The Minister of Finance is required to perform exacting duties. He has no guarantee of employment for any particular time-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hear, hear. Thank goodness.

I think it is hard to
understand why the Minister of Finance and

-who are now taxed as soon as they reach $1,500, having to pay rent and keep their families, there is something radically wrong if others cannot get by on $25,000 a year. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not propose to make an extended comment on the remarks that have been made. It is an old and familiar argument-"soak the rich". I think our income tax scale is a pretty steeply progressive one when you take eighty cents on the top dollar. But no matter how hard you try to soak the rich in this country, or in any other country, you cannot get sufficient revenues from that group, because there are not enough of them.
You get $19 million odd.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I make that statement without fear of contradiction. If you want $90 million or $100 million from that group you cannot get it. That is the fact. It is unearned income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Moreover, we live alongside a country w'hicli is large and powerful and, as I have said before and repeat now, we cannot insulate ourselves completely from conditions as they exist in that country. I agree with my hon. friend that it is desirable to maintain a certain minimum standard of living in this or any other country, but that depends on the level of production in the country, and you cannot legislate for any standard of living. People have to work and produce. You can, it is true, assist in the standard of living by sound fiscal measures, by not imposing a tax structure w'hich deters production, which prevents the undue increase of wealth. That is perfectly true. But you cannot raise the standard of living in this or any other country by a purely "soak the rich" tax policy-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -or talking about a minimum standard of living.

speechtext: But you can, by positive steps taken by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, that may be true. But they are not in my judgment the positive steps suggested by my hon. friend.

Before the resolution carries, there is one point I should like to place before the Minister of Finance with regard to income taxation. The war has now been over for

Income War Tax Act
nearly two years, and I think most Canadians are getting pretty well settled down to normal peacetime living. One of their big problems is that of planning their lives; including of course, their financial affairs; and the government-quite rightly, we in the official opposition believe-is relying on the individual Canadian to do just that-to plan his own affairs, to stand on his own feet. By having as many as possible of our people doing that, we believe we can have the strongest nation. But one important factor to be remembered is that in a plan of that type you must tell the people the facts. They must be given all the information available.
I suggest to the minister that the Canadian people should be given, at as early a day as possible, an approximate idea of the ultimate level of income taxation. The Department of Finance must have some thoughts as to what proportion of our taxation can be raised by the income tax and what percentage of a person's income should be taken from him in that way. Under the proposals of this year, the tax on the first $100 of taxable income is 10 per cent, as hon. members know; on the second $100 it is 12 per cent; on the third, 14 per cent; on the next $100, 16 per cent, and on the next, 18 per cent. Then for taxable income from $500 to $3,500 it is 20 per cent. That is really the rate that applies to the largest group of income taxpayers and I use it to illustrate my submission. Are we to be able to go below that rate? The minister, when he made his budget speech, said at page 2553 of Hansard:
Had our taxes been raised gradually and under normal conditions to their present levels, had they been increased for the productive, peace-time purposes of national development and social security rather than for the unproductive purposes of war, then the present levels migh.t perhaps have been acceptable and tolerable as continuing levels.
He went on to say that such, of course, was not the case, and I quote:
Instead, however, they represent a position to which we have returned after a sudden and unpleasant excursion into painful war-time levels of income tax, and people are still smarting . . . from their war-time experience . . .
Then he uses these significant words:
. . . one must reach the conclusion that those who must bear them-
That is, the income taxes.
-are not ready to support income taxes on the present scale. In fact, I am sure that were our present levels of personal income tax to be continued, they would constitute a serious impediment to a full -working effort and a brake upon the drive and initiative of men and women in all groups and classes.
A reduction has been made, and the minister said with regard to that reduction, at page 2555 of Hansard:
I believe that the verdict of all responsible persons will be that we have gone as far as we can possibly afford to go under the present circumstances.
I think the people of the country still feel that the income tax is too heavy. I do not believe they are prepared to go on paying rates, for example, of 20 per cent in the income range to which I referred a few minutes ago. They feel that they are being heavily shackled even yet by the income taxation. I would ask the minister to let us know, if he can, what the Department of Finance consider to be the normal level for the income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I make no claim to being a prophet, as my hon. friend will appreciate. I assume that the Canadian people must continue to pay their bills, and the amount of tax which will have to be raised will depend upon the amount of expenditures and the amount of government services which the people of Canada, through their elected representatives, demand. I made reference to that in my budget speech. I pointed out that I get continual demands from hon. gentlemen opposite-and sometimes from my own party -for additional expenditures, but I never get any suggestions for reduced expenditures. The reductions in income tax which were made this year, as I said in my budget speech, were as much as I felt I could responsibly recommend with the commitments which Canada has to meet this year. It is true that a great many of those commitments are, I hope, of a temporary nature; and I refer particularly, of course, to the benefits for veterans and so on. But it is difficult to estimate with complete accuracy just what amount those will run to this year. I think the committee will find, when the supplementary estimates are brought in, that in that field as well there will be substantial additional amounts which will have to be provided for. With all these uncertain factors, I am not in a position to say today what I think the income tax scales may be next year or the year after. That, in my judgment, is something which has to be determined each year as we go along; and it will be determined by the demands made by the Canadian people for additional government services of one sort or another. It will depend on the extent to which this or any subsequent government is able to reduce government expenditure but without impairing the essential government services which the people of Canada, through their elected representatives in this house, demand. That is the only answer I can give to my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am now going to answer for myself as Minister of Finance, because it is the minister, in the final analysis, who determines what the tax policy is; and that is as it should be. He is the one who comes before this house and makes tax recommendations and makes recommendations as to the proportion of the total tax load which will be raised by direct taxation'-that is, by income tax on individuals or business concerns-and what will be raised by indirect taxes. I have certain personal view's as to what is a fair proportion between the two. Personally, I should like to see the indirect tax burden reduced as much as possible because, broadly speaking, I feel that it is less fair than direct taxation. The proportion I have struck this year is the best I have been able to arrive at, as I have said to the committee before. I am
not going to make any predictions as to w'hat may be the situation next year; for all I know I may not be minister, probably will not be. This is not something on which I think one should try to make a long-range forecast. Today we estimate that the new income tax structure in a full year w'ill raise something in the order of $425,000,000. My hon. friend can calculate as well as I can what proportion of the total budget is taken from personal income taxes. Then there is a further very substantial portion taken from income taxes on corporations and business concerns. I do not intend to make any predictions. I have view's of my own, but I do not think this is the time to voice them. I can assure my hon. friend that the Department of Finance is not working in the dark, and I hope I am not working in the dark.

Then I am afraid there is not likely to be much reduction in the income tax.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I have no wish to come to the minister's defence. I like him as an individual, but I do not like his economic and social outlook. However, I think he is working in the dark, and as a matter of fact I believe the hon. member for Vancouver South is working in the dark also.
But not as dark as the hon. member for Vancouver East.

Is he in the light?
Mr. MaeINNIS: We shall see about that by and by. Here are people talking about long-term policies, who have washed their hands completely-until yesterday, when we were talking about housing-of directing the economic production of this country. They say production is something with which the government should not be concerned. The production of the country is the wealth out of which the people obtain their living; and that wealth is produced socially. Some get more and some get less of the total produced wealth. Income and other taxes are used to even out the distribution of the national income to some extent. A moment ago. replying to an hon. member over here, the Minister of Finance said the slogan of the C.C.F. was the old slogan of "soak the rich." The only difference between our slogan and his is that his slogan is "soak the poor."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is an easy generality. It is not soaking the poor, and my hon. friend knows better.
Mr. MaeINNIS: Just a moment, now. When someone hits at my hon. friend he does not like it, but he was hitting at us and we

Income War Tax Act
have every right to hit back. He says our slogan is to "soak the rich", and I say he is soaking the poor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I say, don't soak anybody; be fair
Mr. Mm el NX IS:	All right; now we can
agree. Some people are definitely getting soaked, because the minister himself has said that more than one-half of the income earners of this country were receiving incomes below the present level of income tax exemptions. I tell you these people are being soaked, I do not care who is doing it; and because they are being soaked we have to provide various ways of helping them. I am always surprised -that is not correct; I am not surprised, but I wonder at it-when hon. friends to my right ask for a reduction in taxes and then for increases in government services.
Let us look at some of the things we are asking for at the present time, at this present session of parliament. We are asking for better old age pensions. If we are to have better old age pensions the funds to provide them will have to come out of the income of the country, out of the national income. Since we cannot possibly take it out of the people who are already below the income tax exemption levels, it has to come from the incomes of those above the exemption levels. Yesterday we asked for subsidized housing. It is realized that those receiving incomes less than the exemption levels cannot provide themselves with decent housing. If we are to subsidize housing the funds must be provided through taxation. Then we want better health services. If anyone comes along and says we should have better health services, everyone is agreed. Those who are receiving sufficient income to pay for health services can provide their own, but the more than one-half our population whose incomes are below the income tax exemption levels-cannot provide health services for themselves. Consequently, if we are to give better health services that means further expenditures the dominion government has to take on, and it has to come out of taxes. Then several proposals were made that we should make grants in regard to education. I am not trying to be exhaustive in this list; I am just men. tioning a few of these things. So, if we are to do all these things, is there any possibility of doing them and at the same time either reducing or stabilizing taxes?
I think we should be discussing how to increase the total income, the total produced wealth of the country. That is what we should be concerning ourselves with: more houses,
more schools, more machines, more factories, more roads, more transportation. That is the wealth out of which comes the income of our country, which provides the people with their livelihood. The position we are in at the present time is that employers of labour, industrialists, commercial people, financiers, are frightened to death that they may expand their production capacity beyond what can be consumed under our present profit system. On the other hand, the working people are afraid that if they work too hard they will produce too much so that factories will close and there will be unemployment. That is the position in Canada today; that is the position across the line today. Until we assure people that the more they produce, the better off they will be, the happier they will be, the more prosperous they will be, we shall not get anywhere; and we cannot assure our people as long as we leave the production of wealth in the hands of people who are operating industry, not because they are interested in the things produced, but because they are interested in the profit made in the process of production.
I do not suppose there is any use in urging the minister to raise exemption levels, but I do not believe any hon. member will say that a single man can live decently on less than $1,000 a year and prepare himself for the future. If he is an ordinary single man he is only single until he can get himself a better position so that he can marry and bring up a family. Would anyone say today that a married man who is receiving less than $2,000 a year can bring up a family decently, provide them with the healthful living, give them an education which will afford them an opportunity to succeed in the community? No, no one would say that. Then, if we cannot say that, where is the logic in taxing people with incomes of only $750 for a single person and $1,500 for a married person? What is the basis for it? The basis, so far as I can see, is that if the government do not tax these low' incomes they will have to take more from the people who get more. So that, in order that they will not have to take more from the people who get more, they gouge more out of the people who already get less than what is needed for a decent living.

Mr. Chairman, I do not
know how far I would be in order if I were to discuss at this stage of the proceedings the fundamental principles of economics. But I am very much intrigued by some of the arguments which have been made. So far as having light, or being in the dark is concerned, I beg to suggest that I think all three

hon. members who have spoken are in the dark. Of course everyone who speaks thinks he is in the light, and everyone else is in the dark.
Let the blessed sunshine in.
All we can do is to continue working, and to have the best man win.

You are away above the
clouds.
At least I have that advantage.

He has his feet on
the ground, though.
He is closer to the sun.

We seem to have come to
this position, where the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Vancouver South have ended at a point where the only source of money they can see today is that which comes from the taxes they can extract from the people of Canada. That seems to be the only source of funds they can see.
For the last ten years or more we in this corner of the house, without contradiction or refutation by any hon. member, have stated that when a government takes upon itself the power of taxation, or when anyone advocates a policy of taxation to divert part of the national production of the public service, it is not distributing the whole of national production by doing so. In other words I mean that the government assumes, as a fundamental basis, that money and goods are always one and the same thing, and that therefore the only means whereby one can divert part of the national service is to tax somebody, whether it be the poor or the rich, or all of them.
We have challenged that premise again and again, and I do so now. I suggest to the minister that it is possible to reduce taxation and to increase services. Perhaps that sounds like an impossibility, and of course it is impossible under the orthodox policy of finance. But I suggest that there is a policy whereby services can be increased and taxation reduced.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
