speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not interrupt, because it arose out of my attempt to answer earlier this afternoon the argument that the income tax exemptions were too low. That, admittedly, was relevant to a section which deals with

rates of personal income tax. However I had hoped that the committee would not go too far afield, in discussing economic questions. I was drawn into it by being asked to make a forecast on tax policy, which I was not prepared to do.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It was the word "phony" that started it.
I do not intend to pursue it farther, but I did think the point should be made, inasmuch as others had represented their views.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is why I did not interrupt my hon. friend. I thought he was stating his point, and I was content to wait until he had finished.

But I do wish to agree with those who suggest that there should be a basic minimum standard of living below which there should be no tax levies. It may be a matter of opinion as to what that basic minimum should be; but, as I said in my budget speech, I felt that at least every family of four should enjoy a tax-free income of S4.000. The Minister of Finance stated that the standard of living was limited only by the production of the country. Well, we have always ranted and raved about this being one of the richest countries in the world. If that is actually so, I cannot see why every family of four should not be more than able to enjoy an income of $4,000 or thereabouts, tax-free. Certainly this countiy is capable of producing that amount of goods and services.
So far as taxes are concerned, I have already said that can be taken care of in another way. I suggest again that it is possible to increase public services and, at the same time, to reduce taxation. The present economy is based upon the false premise that money equals goods. I suggest that it does not. Therefore it is legitimate for the government, through its own financial institution, to finance a great deal of government services of its own creation, and to issue its own money. To the extent that that can be done, taxation can be avoided.
I suggest that the government would do well to explore the limits of this field, because it will not be long before it will be up against it, so far as finances are concerned. There is no other way I can see than that of accepting some of the suggestions which have originated in this corner of the house.

I think the minister pointed out that he expected on the new level of income tax rates the income tax would yield, for a full year, something over $400 million.

Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was the estimate I gave, yes.
Is that not about equal to the amount of money the government is paying each year by way of interest on its national debt?'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A little less, I should think.

I am not going to take time now, but I suggest that the minister should look into the proposition we have offered time and again. If he were to do so he could save the major portion of the interest he is now paying out on the national debt; if he will just approach public financing with a little new vision, which I am sure he will have after he has been here for a year or two. But he will not have it after he has been here for five or six years, because by that time ideas crystallize along the old orthodox lines.
I suggest that he look into what we have offered, because I am satisfied that if he approaches financing this Canada by the use of national money through the Bank of Canada we have here, he can apply most, if not all of that $400 million of interest he is paying on a huge national debt, to a reduction of income tax, and he will not have to soak anyone on any level of taxation.
I would point out to him that when he begins relieving the burden of income tax of the people of this country he will find that, rich and poor alike, they will give him a lot more production. This country is today labouring under a heavy load of taxation. I have on my file dozens of letters from farmers who say, "If you will just get us a decent reduction of income tax we will produce hogs for you to fill your quotas; we will produce wheat, and other things you require". I believe if the minister will look into this process of using national money and getting that debt paid off, as he can get it paid off. and have the use of the interest, which is now being paid over to coupon clippers, for the reduction of taxes, he will be surprised at what this country will do.

I want to take this opportunity to urge the minister to include the cost of drugs as a medical exemption. Medication is becoming increasingly important in the treatment of disease, and almost every week we are introduced to some new costly and expensive drug which is capable of saving life. In its income tax exemptions the government assumes that an individual can carry four per cent of the cost of medical care in certain categories without an income tax exemption, and then the exemption applies to anything over four per cent. A man earning $2,000 is assumed to be able to carry $80 of medical
expenses without exemption. On a $200 hospital bill he would have an exemption of $120. But that just includes the cost of the doctor, the nurse and the hospital. He may have expenses for X-rays and-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: X-rays are covered.

I am glad to hear they are, but there are many other incidental costs that are not listed. I have a letter from a person who tells me that he has to buy a very expensive drug for his wife. Surgery may occur only once in a lifetime, in an emergency, but drugs such as are mentioned by this man are taken day after day as long as life lasts. In his case it takes twenty-eight per cent of his earnings.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: What is it?

Prostigmine. It is a new drug used for intestinal activation; it is not yet in the dictionaries. I should like the minister to give consideration to including these drugs which are essential to life. I do not think we need to worry that people will include tooth paste and lysol and a lot of things as drugs. I think they could be prescribed by doctors and a listing obtained in the same way that hospital bills and surgery costs are listed. The cost of these things is a heavy burden and handicap on many people, and I should like the minister to give consideration to this suggestion.

Before the resolution carries, I think there are some matters which it would be well to mention for the welfare of our C.C.F. friends and I do it in an absolutely kindly way. They do a lot of talking about things about which they know too little. I should like to refer first to the remarks of the hon. member for Mackenzie. We are in an age of very dangerous thinking. There is a tendency in Great Britain and other places to fall off in production. People there seem to be at their wits' ends to know how to get production in coal and other things which they used to be able to get. There is a reason for all that. Somehow motivation has been destroyed in those countries.
Surely intelligent people in Canada-and Canadians are intelligent-do not want to run into such difficulties. May I refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Mackenzie. There comes to my mind a story of the time when the bolsheviks first took over Russia. They went into a certain city, and in a factory there they found a man who was employed at $20,000 a year. They took that man out and liquidated him because he was getting too much money.
Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member to try to deal with the section under consideration, section 3.

I do not understand why you did not call the hon. member for Mackenzie to order when he was talking as he was. Surely, if a man makes a remark in this chamber we should be permitted to level out matters in some way. I have noticed how one man will be able to present an argument without fault being found and then, when some one else tries to answer it, he is called to order.
I just want to say one thing with regard to this. That man who was getting S20,000 was liquidated, but the next year they were advertising in the markets of Europe for a man at S200.000 to take his place.
There is one thing our C.C.F. friends do not seem to be able to get through their minds. If a nation needs high class men in high places in production it must be ready to motivate those men; otherwise, as the minister says, it will not be very long until they will have no men like that, and will not have the incomes to tax.
I should like to make just one remark with regard to what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver East. The hon. member would have to make half a dozen long speeches in order to support that stand. Let us take the railroad situation as an example. The hon. member is asking if the taking over of the Canadian National Railways added anything to the amount of money in Canada with which to run the railroad. That is real wealth.

That is just the kind of thing I had hoped the hon. member for Vancouver East would say. Just two or three minutes before, he was pointing out the fact that the producers in Canada and United States were in desperate alarm lest they have 
too much production. Those producers are private owners! How can the hon. member get any sense out of his stand?
We can get the production we need in Canada if we only motivate private producers. What we need is a financial system able to distribute our production at fair prices.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

the 1947 and 1948 taxation years to expenditures on groups of wells drilled to locate stratigraphic traps.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall give a brief explanation. Then' I expect that some hon members will have some questions to ask. The general purpose of this resolution is to extend, for the calendar year 1948, the wartime tax concessions allowed to oil, gas and mining operators. The special provision relating to deep-test oil wells has been broadened slightly to allow these benefits to those who will undertake extensive expenditure to locate stratigraphic traps. Hon. members who are experts in the field of geology will understand what this means.
The form in which these tax concessions will be given for 1948 will be changed as a result of the absence of the excess profits tax. In future the expenditure will be allowed as a write-off out of income rather than in the form of a tax credit appropriate to the prevailing tax rate. It is necessary, however, to continue a tax credit for deep-test wells over and above the write-off provision.

On this resolution I wish
to refer to the repeal last year of section 8, subsection 5 of the Income War Tax Act, which allowed a deduction from tax of forty per cent of the contributions to prospecting syndicates prospecting for base metals and strategic minerals. As I say, that subsection was repealed last year. I wish to urge the minister to restore the provision and expand it. I suggest to him particularly that he expand its scope from base metals and strategic minerals to include all minerals and metals and more particularly gold. Second, I suggest to him that when he restores it he should remove the limitation of the section in two other ways. At. the present time it is limited to partnerships. An individual grubstaking a prospector cannot take advantage of the provision which was in the act. There was also a limitation of $500 on the contribution which could be made to any one prospecting syndicate.
The minister and the committee know more than I of the value to the Canadian economy in having a high production of gold. He knows the difficulty under which the gold mining industry is suffering at. present. Just recently the government announced an immigration policy, which, if it is to have any practical effect in line with the promises which it contained, will require a tremendous development to the north of our settled areas. Any such development would have to be primarily based upon the development of
mines in the area. Once the mines are established, the other settlements that follow come in.
One of the great advantages of the restoration of this section would be that it would popularize our mining industry among individuals who are not engaged solely in the business of mining. At present a mining company gets, under the resolution the minister is proposing, some tax concession for exploration expenses, but those engaged in the industry are not so greatly in need of concessions to interest them in it as are individuals, businessmen, doctors, lawyers and private citizens who might, as a side issue, wish to offer help in the grubstaking of miners.
Briefly I should like to refer the minister to an article that appeared in the Saturday Evening Post of May 17. 1947, by Averell Harriman, Secretary of Commerce of the United States. He points this out in a long article which has an arresting title, and one which I think will hearten everyone in the house on another subject. Speaking to his own people in the United States, he heads the article, "We must import to live." He goes on to cite many examples of shortages in important industrial metals which have arisen in the United States owing to the tremendous drain they have put upon them. He says that the United States have to look outside their own boundaries for the supply of metals and minerals. If there is anything in what the Secretary of Commerce of the United States says, there should be a great future for new development of our mining industry in Canada if only to supply the increased market that he foresees by reason of their becoming a "have-not" nation in respect of minerals, instead of a "have" nation as they have been up to the present time. These reasons will commend themselves to the minister, and I am sure he knows them now. I just mention them in passing.
1 want to turn to a particular reason I am suggesting why this provision, which stood for several years during the war, should be reintroduced. I have had correspondence from the British Columbia and Yukon Chamber of Mines, from the manager of the organization. Mr. Woodside, who is a man of more than fifty years' experience in mining in Canada and who has for the past twenty-nine years conducted a prospectors school in the winter in Vancouver. The number in the last class this winter was 150. I should think his opinion would be a valued one as to conditions in British Columbia. He says that this provision, to his personal knowledge, during the war was particularly useful in stimulating the

Income War Tax Act
contribution of money for grubstaking prospectors in British Columbia. He also says that it has been more useful in British Columbia, perhaps, than in other parts of Canada for two important reasons. First of all, the cost of prospecting in British Columbia is very high because of the difficult terrain and the difficult transportation conditions. I have three examples which may be of interest to the minister. In one area one prospector went out this year and his grubstake was $2,000. In another area not far away on the map two required $6,000 for their season's financing.
In the Yukon, which is, of course, just north of British Columbia, another party of two needed $16,000 for the supply of equipment and other expenses before they were able to go into the field. I understand that these conditions do not obtain to the same extent in eastern Canada. Second, prospecting in British Columbia is not done primarily by mining companies which already are provided for in the present regulations. In British Columbia, perhaps because we have not as big a money market as there is in Toronto, more than half the prospecting is done by individual prospectors who have to raise their own money and are not on salary from mining companies. That is another reason why this provision was particularly useful out in the west. I suggest to the minister that what is being done for an incorporated company might well be done for the partnership or individual who grubstakes a prospector in Canada and my specific suggestions to him are these:
1.	That he restore the principle of the old section.
2.	That he extend it to all mines and metals, including gold, and not restrict it, as it was during the war, to base metals and strategic minerals.
3.	That he include not only partnerships but individuals who may grubstake prospectors by themselves. I do not see any tremendous difference between three or four men doing it and one man doing it.
4.	That he raise the limit of the contribution for any single operation. It was, as I understand, a total of $5,000. with a limit of $500 on any individual contribution, and I suggest that perhaps he keep the limit of $5,000 and raise the $500 limit. I will not name the figure because I am not as competent as the officials to judge in that regard.
5.	I suggest, finally, that he give consideration to helping the prospector who grubstakes himself by working in the winter in the mines

or in some industrial employment in Vancouver, using the money he earns in the winter to go into the field during the summer.
I am aware of some administrative difficulties that would arise in the latter case, but very likely a scheme could be worked out if the principle were established.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This exemption was a most unusual and exceptional one which was allowed during war time to stimulate the search for strategic minerals. At the time it was put in it was asserted that prospectors might not be willing to go out and search for this particular type of mineral unless they were financed, and I suppose that is natural. The provision was put in the law, therefore, whereby an individual who contributed to one of these prospecting associations, syndicates or mining partnerships, registered or otherwise recognized under the laws of any province or territory of Canada, organized for the purpose of prospecting for minerals, could deduct his contribution from his taxable income in the same way as he could deduct a contribution made to a hospital or a charitable organization. I am informed that it actually took the form of a tax credit. That was an exceptional provision. and it was felt that it was not one that should be retained in the permanent tax structure. I have voiced the view in this house on other occasions that I had serious doubts myself as to the wisdom of this particular form of tax concession. I thought it was so exceptional that it should not be maintained longer than the period for which it had been put in, namely the w'ar, and it was dropped at the end of 1945. I am sure I would not feel justified in reinstating it at this time. Any encouragement that may be needed for prospecting for minerals, whether base metals or gold mining, should be given in some other form lhan this special form of tax credit or deduction.
What form of assistance is there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should think the ordinary incentive that exists in the case of any other businessman who goes out and looks for something he thinks is profitable. Frankly, I have a constitutional objection to setting up special classes of tax exemptions, and this is one that did not apply to any special type of enterprise. It was put in because it was asserted during the war that perhaps prospectors w'ould not look for these minerals, which were badly needed, unless there was this inducement to investors to grubstake them. I think the investor who is now prepared to grubstake a prospector must accept the same tax position as any other investor.

Income War Tax Act

I tried to anticipate the minister's known feelings on both these points. First of all, I did try to indicate that there was perhaps some continuing need in Canada on other than war grounds for stimulating the interest of the people generally in prospecting, and for seeing to it that prospectors did get out. Second, I knew his often expressed view that there should be as few exceptions from a tax as possible. I am not asking the minister to make any exception from the tax or to allow any tax credit which he is not already allowing under clause 5, as I understand it. If a company can get some relief because it is in the mining business-and I thoroughly approve that-I see no reason why an individual or partnership should not have, not greater, but similar relief. I do not ask that it be in the form of a tax credit, for instance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, but it is the business of the mining company to search for minerals and get them. The tax relief here is to you or me or any other citizen who may want to take a chance and invest a few hundred dollars in a prospecting syndicate. I have voiced the view before-and I still hold it-that this particular tax concession lent itself to the sale of stock in those prospecting syndicates about as much as it did to giving persons an incentive to go out and look for the minerals. It is completely different from the tax concessions given mining companies and oil companies actually engaged in the business of searching for and producing minerals. This is a concession that was given to anyone who wanted to put up a few dollars in a prospecting syndicate, which might be nothing but a syndicate organized by a stock promoter to go out and pound a few rocks or cut a few trails to see if he could find minerals. Probably it was justified in war time, but I have held the view very strongly-and I still hold it-that it is not the type of concession that can be justified in peace time under normal conditions. It was dropped at the end of 1945 and I do not think it should be continued.

One more word, then. There is no reason that I' can see why the principle to which the minister has referred should be so rigidly applied as to stop one class of persons engaged in mining from enjoying the same benefits as another class.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does not.

The mere fact that it is the business of the mining company engaged in exploration-it is their principal business- cannot be of as much importance as the need which I think exists, and of which I do not think there is any doubt, what we should promote the development of one of our chief natural resources. ' When the minister talks about administrative difficulties in working out one of these provisions, I must say I am not at all impressed. For instance, there are,
I understand, provisions in the mining legislation for the issuance of prospectors identification cards. There are many ways, I feel sure, in which anyone who had adopted the principle could get over any of the administrative difficulties which surround it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not pleading administrative difficulties at all. I say that the concession is objectionable on other grounds.
The minister referred to the possibility that the provision might be used to promote the sale of shares in a syndicate rather than to do prospecting.

speechtext: Any mining syndicate or exploration syndicate which is registered as such can go out, sell stock and get contributions from individuals. There is no way in which the Department of National Revenue can check on an enterprise of that kind. I know that. I again repeat that I think this special and unusual type of incentive tax concession is not justified under peacetime conditions.

I should like to correct one statement which the Minister of Finance made with regard to mining companies going out and getting these claims. In my experience- and 1 have been in the north for a long time -you would not have had any mines at all if it had been left to the mining companies to stake these mines. It has been the prospectors and syndicates such as those which the hon. member spoke about, that found those mines in the early days.

I did not say the mining companies were sending them out. M}' hon.

You have not said anything yet.

One more thing I should like to remind the minister of is that some of these small prospectors must receive some encouragement, because today they are not going into the bush in our northern country. desirable or fair to give it to the individual prospector. Perhaps someone else may think differently, but I do not.

I had no intention of speaking on this matter because I know' very little about it; but two things the minister has said prompt me to mention two things and to ask him a question. It seems to me that the important question is whether or not we think we are, under our present laws, getting the utmost exploration and the utmost bringing in of new minerals. It does not seem to me to be important whether we are in peace time or war time. The question is whether we feel we are getting what we should get.
The second thing is, it seemed to me that the minister confused the issue by raising this question of stock sales. I am no more fond of stock promotions than hon. gentlemen to my left; they have no monopoly on a dislike for that kind of thing. But I want to suggest that I believe there are efficient organizations in the provinces trying to stop that kind of thing, and personally I should not have thought that was a conclusive reason. I am not offering any suggestions; I am not asking the minister to restore the tax. I merely say
it seems to me that the important thing is whether we are to get the maximum amount of work done to bring new mines into production.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is, I agree, the important thing.

That is the underlying
feature.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right. I do not think we should, but perhaps we ought to subsidize the prospectors who go into the bush. Then perhaps the provinces, which derive large revenues from the development of mines, should take some steps to 'encourage prospecting. My point is that this type of tax concession to individuals, not to the prospector himself, but to individual investors who are willing to gamble four or five hundred dollars in a prospecting syndicate, should not be given special tax concessions. I say they should not get that tax concession in peace time. I am repeating myself a great many times, but that is a view I have held for a long time.

Perhaps I had better make it clear at the start that I am interested only in paragraphs (a) and (b) of this resolution, dealing with oil and natural gas, on which the minister made a brief statement when we first considered this resolution. It seems to me that the whole tax picture as far as the oil industry is concerned is needlessly confused; and I am sorry to say that, as far as I am concerned, the statement made by the minister this evening has only added to the opaqueness, or perhaps I should say the opacity, of that picture. At any rate I am just a little more confused than ever.
In addition to the general confusion that exists as far as the taxation of the oil industry is concerned, there is also the point that the taxes on that industry, or the concessions from taxes, are on a year to year basis, which makes it extraordinarily difficult for the oil operator to plan his future operations or to know where he stands. As an example, the exemption from duty of pipe and oil drilling equipment is provided at the present time under the omnibus bill and will continue until that bill expires. What will happen in connection with the duty on pipe and other oil drilling equipment after the omnibus bill ceases to have effect, nobody knows; and of course it is a matter of extreme interest to oil operators as to what the situation will be.
I have several questions, I am sorry to say, that I should like to ask the minister. The first is whether he is prepared to make any statement as to what the situation will be as far as duty is concerned on pipe and oil drill-

ing equipment, as to whether the government have given that matter any consideration, and whether or not they are willing to make the present tariff concessions part of the regular tariff schedules. I must say I brought up this matter when the omnibus bill was being discussed. I thought that was the proper time for it, but I was ruled out of order and referred to the budget, and as a result I am bringing it up at this time. In that connection I should like from the minister, if possible, a statement as to whether or not a particular piece of equipment known as a heater treater can or will be included among the particular articles of oil drilling equipment that are exempt from duty at the present time.
The oil picture in Alberta is much brighter now than it was this time a year ago. During 1946 I think in the neighbourhood of 190 oil wells were drilled in Alberta, of which some fifty were producers. In 1947 a more active drilling programme has been in progress, owing to quite a considerable extent to the fact that the price of crude oil has been allowed to rise, following the removal of subsidies, by an amount equal to the subsidy which was withdrawn. Quite a number of wells have been brought into production in the plains area of Alberta and Saskatchewan, particularly in the Lloydminster area. More important than that, however, is the fact that a new field of high grade oil, at a fairly reasonable depth of something between five and six thousand feet, has been brought into production at Leduc, where there are three producing wells at the present time. From present indications it seems that we have at Leduc in Alberta another oil field comparable with the Turner valley and, we hope, exceed*-ing it.
All this progress, however, has not removed the need for more incentive to encourage drilling. I think it is quite apparent to everyone that the finding of large oil fields would have several beneficial results as far as Canada is concerned. In the first place, it would bring down the cost of oil and oil derivatives such as gasoline and so forth, in which nearly all our citizens are interested. In addition, it would materially ease our foreign exchange difficulties as far as United States funds are concerned, because one of the chief causes of our loss of foreign exchange is the amount of oil we have to import. As a matter of fact, a fair number of reasonable oil fields would also do away with the difficulty the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply spoke of the day before yesterday, as far as the shortage of fuel oil is concerned.
Without going into that point farther, as I say I think it is quite clear that the dis-

covery of oil fields in Canada is a matter of major importance to the country. The fact that we do not have more oil fields than at present is, at least to a large extent, due to the taxation and other policies which have been pursued by the present government. In other words, the tax structure has not been such as to encourage the drilling of oil wells, and more incentive along that line is still needed.
I should like to refer to the tax concessions which I suggested last year, and which have been suggested by the oil men for a considerable time, and to ask the minister what consideration has been given to these suggestions during the past year and why no action has been taken on them. First, it was requested that the fifty per cent tax drawback or deduction for deep-test wells be extended to apply to wells drilled in the plains areas. As far as I know, nothing has been done in that regard, and I should like the minister to say why nothing has been done and why that very reasonable request has not been accepted. The second request was for a greater depletion allowance. Last year and the previous year that allowance was 33| per cent. In the United States, oil operators are given a depletion allowance of up to fifty per cent and, furthermore, they can carry it forward or backward. In a year when they have no net income they can save the depletion allowance on the oil produced and use it in a future year; or if their tax arrears have not been settled they can carry the allowance back. It seems to me that if we are properly to encourage the drilling of oil wells a depletion allowance at least equal to that received by our chief competitors immediately to the south, in the United States, should be allowed to our own oil operators.
Third, the request was that all drilling expenses including costs of permits and leasing, geological and geophysical exploration, and all that sort of thing be allowed as tax deductions. The fourth request was that all concessions at present allowed should be included in the permanent tax structure, so that operators would know where they stand and be able to make plans for the future.
I have a few more remarks to make on another related subject, namely in connection with natural gas, but I should like to have the minister answer these questions first.
Before the minister speaks, may I add a few words?

What I shall say will be along the same lines as those followed by the hon. member for Calgary East. What I say is not so much by way of complaint, as to urge that I do not think the taxing authorities have ever had a complete and sufficient knowledge of our problem out there.
There is no doubt whatever about the importance of oil in our economy. I am sure no one would deny that, for a moment; and if we can but increase that production we shall have gone a long way. The Turner valley, our one large field, is on the downgrade, although last year it produced seven or eight million barrels; and those were 40-gallon barrels. After all, that is a lot of oil; and it is of high quality, about 40 gravity.
We have had a most intensive search and many wells have been drilled. They are seeking there, not only to continue development in the foothills, but to find oil in the plains area comparable, we will say, with the immense supply in the state of Texas. That drilling is much shallower.
For instance, today to drill a well in the Turner valley will cost at least $200,000. Wells at present being drilled are being drilled at a cost of anywhere from $25,000 up to roughly $60,000, as in the case of the Leduc field, which has been mentioned. That is exclusive of the production equipment.
It is fortunate that the Imperial Oil Company have discovered what appears to be a new field, in which they have drilled three wells. It is most unusual, but we find that all are excellent producing wells. Number two blew in during the course of the present week. But, as I have said, they have had three out of three. They can be drilled for roughly $60,000 each. That area is held largely by the bigger companies; none of the smaller independent companies are in there. They may have a half-section, but the greater part of the ground is held by these larger companies.
What is the tax position? Remember, we are dealing with something that is called an income tax. I am leaving out for the moment the concession on marginal wells or deep-test wells, to which reference has been made. We will put it this way, and say that a group of members in the House of Commons have formed a company and subscribed $200,000. We take that money and drill an oil well, and from it we get back the $200,000. Things are going very well, so we say, "We will certainly begin to drill another one." We drill another one and it is a duster-a dry well. The $200,000 we got out of the first well is taxed. We have lost it in the second well; and yet we have paid tax on income for the whole of that $200,000, less depletion allowance.
I hope the minister will correct me if I make a single mistake in what I am saying. Remember, I have said that I am disregarding depletion allowances at certain percentages, and I am not talking about deep-test wells, although I shall, later on.
So, we in the House of Commons who have formed the company have spent the S200.000 and we have got it back. Then we have put it into another well, but we have not got a cent from it. But we have had to pay income tax on that first $200,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I want to learn more about this oil business.

I am trying to deal with the oil business in the province from which I come and from which many hon. members over here come. What has happened? We have a field called Turner valley. You may have read of great productions here, there or elsewhere, and at this great distance Turner valley has been regarded as a small thing. May I say that in itself it is one of the largest fields ever discovered in North America, and I know that will come as a great surprise to some people. The average cost of drilling a well there is about S200.000, and they are now drilling below 10.000 feet at the north end with the cost running $250,000 and higher. Imperial Oil drilled one up

Income War Tax Act
between Edson and Cadomin which cost over a million dollars, and it was a dry hole. They went down 13,000 feet.
What I am trying to show is that the people out there are not fiddling with this thing; they are trying very hard to develop something. I admit they are doing it for profit, that is the incentive; that is the reason they are there. If they make a profit and are able to supply western Canada with oil, then we shall all be infinitely better off. With a production of 8,000.000 odd barrels last year from the one field, they could supply only Alberta and part of Saskatchewan. Before the war, we had advanced as far as Brandon and were able to supply that part of the Manitoba market, but that is not true today. I should like the minister to explain paragraph (c), which reads in part:
. . . and that the amended provisions relating to expenditures on deep-test oil wells apply in respect of the 1947 and 1948 taxation years to expenditures on groups of wells drilled to locate stratigraphic traps.
Do I correctly interpret that as meaning that the same deduction, assistance if you like, which in times gone by was given to deep-test wells, so-called, will now apply to wells drilled on the prairie structures?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not necessarily. If my hon. friend wishes I will explain what is meant by this extension of the provision which existed last year. When it was suggested by the Department of Mines and Resources that the tax concession contained in the section which is now in the act and which is being extended for 1948 should include groups of wells drilled to locate stratigraphic traps I asked them what that was. They have given me an explanation which I shall be obliged to read to t.he committee because I am not a geologist. Probably it will be entirely clear to those who, like my hon. friend, have a knowledge of oil wells. This is the explanation given me by the Department of Mines and Resources:
The term "deep test" has been restricted so far to an exceptionally deep or costly well proposed to be drilled in potential oil bearing territory to prove or disprove the commercial productivity of a geological horizon on some deeply buried dome, anticline or other significant geological structure. The most probable productive part of such a structure is its summit, and the location of this can generally be determined from a detailed geological examination of the bedrock exposures in the area, from deep holes previously drilled, or from a seismic survey. The possibilities of such a structure can generally be determined from the results of a single deep well.
A "stratigraphic trap" on the other hand, is not a structural dome, but an oil or gas reservoir formed in a porous formation such as sandstone
or clastic limestone as a lenticular bed a pinch-out, or a somewhat similar type of deposit, formed along an ancient buried shore line, or as some deltaic or flood-plain deposit in potential oil bearing territory. The tilting of these strata causes a separation of the gas, oil and water by gravity, with the gas and oil rising to the up-dip side. The escape of these is prevented by the porous horizon being sealed off by an overlapping younger shale or other impervious sedimentary formation which was deposited in an advancing sea. Such porous reservoir sands have been deposited from various sources and are therefore apt to be very erratic, irregular and patchy in distribution, and inconsistent in composition and thickness. The location or outline of such deposits cannot be determined from a geological examination of surface bedrock outcrops or from a seismic survey, nor can this be established from a single drill hole, but only by the drilling of a series of holes, seldom less than six or nine in number. The production from any one hole is apt to be much smaller than that derived from the tapping of a structural high of a potential oil-bearing structure.
I do not pretend to understand the technical significance of that, but I understand that it is the type of exploration where one has to drill a series of holes, not so deep as deep-test holes,- because of the particular formation, and it is proposed to extend the special tax concession to that type of test well.
How does one know when he is drilling on one of those structures?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know. I would have to get another memorandum from the Department of Mines and Resources.

Strange as it may seem, I understand what the minister has just read. However, there is one very great error in that. It says that when you are dealing with a dome, if you hit the top you get the best production. You do not; you get gas and that is all you get. The way oil is laid down in these anticlines is with water at the bottom, the oil next and the gas at the top. What you do is to drill down the edge and cause the pressure of the gas to force the oil up. There is that difference in what the minister has just read.
What I am talking about are areas like the Princess field or the areas around Brooks or Taber, where a comparatively large amount of money has been spent. It is not a question of single holes. Imperial Oil started off with at least a five-well programme and now they have a thirty-well programme. They struck oil in the first hole, but that was just their good luck.
If I understand aright what the minister says, if the company which I have formed in this House of Commons went down to the
Income War Tax Act

Gleichen reserve and started drilling where we thought there was a stratigraphic trap; if we started off with a five-well programme we would be doing exactly what the minister has said. What I am trying to do and what I hope the minister will see is that if we had that sort of thing, then we would receive the same concessions and assistance as is given to deep-test wells.
May I say one thing which is logical and which proves everything that I have been trying to say. We are looking for new oil wells. It does not make any difference if we find one below the other or if we find them side by side. Of course the side by side ones will be at less depth and much more inexpensive than the. so-called deep-test wells. In other words, the whole logic of the situation compels me to think-and I have never heard any answer to it

I mentioned this last year, but I have not had any answer that if assistance is to be given in the seeking of new fields, new oil, it should not be perpendicular, that the fields should lie one under another. It seems to me to be infinitely more simple if we find them side by side and at shallower depth.
I was down here long before I became a member of parliament on this same question, and I was well received by Doctor Eaton, Doctor Clark, and some of these splendid gentlemen who belong to the minister's department. I have always felt and I still feel that you have one of the finest geologists in Canada right here in the person of Doctor Hume. His advice is well worth while; he is a splendid gentleman. He has a tremendous number of things to do in a geological way. He has an immense area of country to cover in charge of exploratory parties, and so on. He must cover immense areas of ground, but it does seem to me-and I wish someone would answer this question-that if we are to assist somebody who is looking for oil deep down, we should assist the chap, the company or the corporation who is going to find it at shallower depth. If you have two fields side by side they are just as good as if you had two in the form of one superimposed upon the other with this impervious rock in between. We can talk about these seismic surveys and all these other things. If you are drilling in a place where you think there is a stratigraphic trap you will find that there is only one discoverer of oil. and that is the drill. Everybody in the oil business knows that. You can shoot all the dynamite you like all over the place, but you will find that at depth you quite often get salt water. In that you are lucky sometimes, because usually you get nothing. Oil
is found only by the drill. No greater boon could come to Canada than that we should become largely suppliers of our own oil.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall endeavour to answer some of these questions. I agree that it would be most desirable and helpful to Canada if we could discover additional oil sources, and it is for that reason that this particular tax concession, which has been in the law. was put in and is being continued. As to why it is not extended to other types of exploration, the reason is contained in the section itself. Whether it is an adequate reason is, of course, another matter. But this applies only, in the language of the statute where, under 10 (b):
The taxpayer could not be reasonably expected to drill the oil well unless permitted to deduct at least fifty per centum of the expenditures in connection therewith from tax.
In other words, this particular type of well is, I understand, a very expensive operation; it runs, as my hon. friend has said, to a million dollars for one well. The other type of well, shallow well, does not cost anything like that amount, and it was felt that for that type of well the prospector, the oil company, the wild-catter would be within his financial means and could be expected to undertake it. This special incentive was given to induce the drilling of these very expensive wells which would otherwise not be undertaken. five per cent tax on dividends leaving Canada from subsidiaries to foreign parents. The present resolution, then, imposes a tax of five per cent where none was imposed before, but it still leaves the parent subsidiary dividends bearing a lower rate than that which applies generally to dividends leaving Canada. 9. That funding securities received in respect of an accrued right to interest, dividends or other payments of an income nature or in respect of the extinguishment of a shareholder's preference to the declaration of dividends for past periods be taxable as income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I had better explain this resolution, because I have an amendment to move.
Resolution No. 9 as amended makes provision for taxation in two directions. The first part of the resolution makes taxable in the year of receipt the value of a security received in respect of an accrued right to receive interest, dividends or other payments of an income nature. The house is aware that companies which have been in financial difficulties frequently issue what are commonly called funding securities covering arrears of interest on its bonds that the company has been unable to meet in the past. This interest, if it had been paid, would, of course, have been income to the bondholders in each year in which received. When the bondholder receives a new bond covering arrears of interest he has, in effect, received the interest in one lump sum, although it is received in the form of a promise to pay. There has been some doubt regarding the present law as to whether the recipient of the funding security is taxable on the receipt of the security or whether the tax liability is deferred until the time when the security is redeemed, that is, when the company actually pays cash to the bondholder. It seems clear that the practice should be to have the tax liability fall in the year in which
the funding security is received by the bondholder, and this is what is being proposed in the present resolution.
The second part of the amended resolution deals with the premium received by a shareholder upon the redemption of his shares. At present the premium upon redemption is deemed to be a dividend. The proposed amendment is that the premium shall be taxable as income. The change in wording has the effect of making a corporation taxable in respect of premium received, whereas under the present law the corporation is not- taxable because the premium is deemed to be a dividend and, as the committee knows, dividends paid from one corporation to another are exempt from tax in the hands of the receiving corporation.
In the case of funding securities, this will relate only to interest-bearing securities and not preferred shares and the like or shares which are issued in connection with arrears of cumulative preferred dividends. I would ask my colleague the Minister of National Revenue to move the amendment which I am proposing

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
I move, Mr. Chairman:
That paragraph 9 of the resolution to amend the Income War Tax Act now before the committee be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"9. That funding securities received on or after January 1, 1947, in respect of an accrued right to interest, dividends or other payments of an income nature and premiums received on or after May 31, 1947, on redemption of shares by a corporation, be taxable as income."

Part of what I had to criticize has been removed by this amendment, but I think it is open to this criticism, if I understand the amendment which has just been proposed. It seems to me that what it means in simple language is this. Assuming I have a bond bearing interest and, we will say, the company has been unable to pay that interest for a period of ten years, and then some refunding is done for the accrued interest which is owing to me; had I received that interest through the period of the ten years it would have affected only' my gross income or taxable income to perhaps only a comparatively small extent. But remember I have not had it, and now I receive the shock of getting it all at one time, not in money but in a promise to pay, so that my tax in that year, it seems to me, is unduly enhanced, if I may use that expression.
Put, it another way. Suppose I had $100 a year coming to me during the ten years. At the end of ten years it is $1,000. and at that time there is a reorganization and a refunding issue is put up. I do not get the $1,000 but a

Income War Tax Act
new form of bond or preference share or security or something of that, kind, and that is only a promise to pay. But. that $1,000, added to my income in that year, since we have an ascending scale of income taxation, means that I am unfairly struck all at once. I am asking the minister if he does not think he might spread that burden over the period during which I otherwise would have received the money had the corporation been able to pay it, or for some lesser period. It strikes me as being unfair to the individual who has not received interest payments, on which perhaps he has relied during those years when he has had to borrow other money at a greater rate, it may be, to maintain himself and his business, or whatever it may be. It is severe that you should say, "In the year 1957 we are giving you a security, a promise to pay, in lieu of money you did not receive, which will be in the same amount, and you will add that, to your taxable income during that year." That is something worth the minister's consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Resolutions 10, 11, 12 and
13 all relate to the special provisions concerning so-called private companies which were put in the law following the recommendations of the Ives commission. The committee may recall that legislation was introduced in 1945 dealing with the recommendations of the Ives commission regarding the position of shareholders of closely-held companies. The problem arose out of the situation faced by the estate of the chief shareholder of these companies having to meet the liability for succession duties upon the death of the main owner of the business. The legislation made provision for the payment of a tax by the corporation on its undistributed income. Thereafter a payment of a dividend out of this accumulated surplus which had been specially taxed was free from further tax when paid out to the shareholder.
As the law now stands, a company with more than fifty shareholders cannot qualify for the benefits of the legislation. Resolution No. 10 proposes that, the limit on the number of shareholders be raised to seventy-five. Cases have been brought, to the government's attention where, through various reasons, the

Income War Tax Act
shareholding has been moderately widened, with the passing of the years, although such company is still, in fact, a privately held corporation. It seemed reasonable, therefore, that the terms of the legislation might be made less rigid in order that many deserving cases which now are disqualified may be enabled to come under the terms of the law and pay the special tax.

I want to make objection, not to the increase to seventy-five, but to the increase to any specified number of shareholders. The minister has touched on the difficulties which the department has found in applying this to one or other of the various companies which have applied. But as I understand it, the number of shareholders is fixed as of April 29, 1941. thereby rendering an injustice to one company which happens to have had more of its shareholders die prior to that date than might die later.
Dealing with this amendment in 1945, may I say that I know of one company in which one man died leaving thirty-two heirs and in that fashion counted his company out of taking the benefit of this act. I suggest to the minister that the true purpose back of the act as passed in 1945 was to give certain rights to closely held corporations, provided that they had less than fifty shareholders; but instead of that date being fixed as of April 29, 1941, it .should be fixed as of the original date of incorporation if at that time it conformed in other respects with the definition of a private company. Then, if thereafter any of the original shareholders remain as of the date of April 29, 1941, and if the remainder of the shareholders are successors to the original ones, that company might enjoy the benefit of the resolution; because, as years go by and the shareholders die off, this same company may still continue to have its surplus undistributed and each family in turn may make the strenuous efforts to avoid distribution to which the Ives commission referred. If that is the case, the last surviving man or his family upon his death, finds it even more onerous to face the difficulties. Therefore I suggest that the minister, between now and when the amendments come in, might give consideration to that. In the meantime I am going to ask the department to look at page 62 of the Ives report and let us have some facts as to the number of companies which have taken advantage of this amendment of 1945 and the amount of money collected from them.

As the committee will have appreciated from listening to the hon. member for Grey-Bruce, the law is intricate, and this is inevitably so because of the very nature of the subject being dealt with. In arriving at the amount of undistributed income, the law has to provide for the adding up of surplus earned since 1917. Since that date there have been many changes in our law, and the present amendment arises through the fact that at one time in the

Criminal Code
history of income tax there was a special provision relating to a class of company known as "family corporations". Shareholders of these family corporations were not taxable on the dividends received from them. The privilege of paying out of a family corporation dividends tax-free continued up to the end of 1942. It is necessary, therefore, in calculating undistributed income on hand at the end of 1939 for purposes of the present tax to exclude therefrom the amount which, subsequently to 1939, was paid out tax-free in the hand of the recipients. The present amendment gives effect to this exclusion.
